paper_design_summary: Formative work comprised three interviews with E1 representing the E1-E7 teaching team and a separate prototype evaluation with six teachers (I1-I6; pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2). Experiment I compared LitLinker (GLM-4) with a chatbot using the same model in 16 students, using counterbalanced within-person task-system orders without stated random allocation and blinded expert ratings on seven lesson-plan criteria (pp. 10-12, Sections 5.1-5.4.1). Experiment II interviewed nine final-system users (E1-E5, E8-E11) and also reused I1-I6's prototype feedback on unchanged features (pp. 13-14, Sections 6.1-6.2).

ai_tool.name_model: LitLinker (multi-agent system built on Zhipu GLM-4 with RAG over a context pool) vs Zhipu LLM web application
ai_tool.how_used: LitLinker recommends interdisciplinary contexts, analyzes texts against a chosen context, and generates a course plan, introduction, and activities; the baseline is a general chatbot. Participants freely chose whether, when, and how to use the tools.

task.description: As a sixth-grade Chinese language teacher, identify an interdisciplinary context, integrate at least three of eight reading materials with it, and write a course plan with proposed activities
task.duration: 30 minutes per task; about 90 minutes per participant in total

outcomes.measure_detail: One experienced Chinese language teacher (E1) rated all outcomes in randomized order, blind to condition, on a 7-point scale; seven criteria in Figure 4. The abstract describes this as integration depth of different subjects.

eligibility.reason: Experiment I analyzes the same 16 students in both conditions, below the 50-person threshold (p. 10, Section 5.1; p. 11, Table 2). Task-system orders are counterbalanced but random allocation is not stated; explicit randomization concerns the expert's rating order (pp. 10-11, Sections 5.2-5.3). Seven expert ratings are scored on the produced lesson plans (pp. 11-12, Sections 5.3-5.4.1 and Figure 4). The qualitative foundational interviews, prototype evaluation, and final-system interviews do not add people to that comparison or supply an eligible randomized output-score contrast (pp. 3-5, Sections 3.1-3.2; pp. 13-14, Sections 6-6.2). Retain in the screening report as a small experiment with unresolved assignment; no qualifying context class is established.

one_line_finding: In a within-subject comparison of 16 students, LitLinker lesson plans scored higher than baseline-chatbot plans on Completion (5.56 vs 4.19, p = 0.02) and, not significantly, on Subject Integration (4.63 vs 3.56, p = 0.34), but lower on Content Alignment (4.25 vs 5.69, p = 0.22) (p. 12, Section 5.4.1, Figure 4).
notes: Experiment I is coded other because random assignment of participants or task-system order is not documented; the only explicit randomization concerns E1's rating order (pp. 10-11, Sections 5.2-5.3). Directions describe the printed arm means. Only Completion is statistically significant among the seven output ratings; the source prose calls baseline advantages significant despite its larger printed p values (p. 12, Section 5.4.1 and Figure 4). S3 counts E1 as the direct foundational interviewee and describes the E1-E7 team's indirect contribution; S4 records I1-I6 separately, and their reused feedback in S2 must not be treated as a new independent sample (pp. 3-5, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 14, Section 6.2; p. 16, Section 7.4).
